meta.title: Transformer attention as a domain clustering tool for space survey machine learning pipelines

abstract: Modern astronomical surveys generate imaging datasets containing billions of objects, requiring automated machine learning (ML) pipelines. As survey sizes increase, analyzing these datasets at full scale becomes increasingly challenging. Methods that can group visually similar objects and reduce large datasets through clustering are therefore of practical importance. In this work we investigate the clustering behavior of embeddings produced by transformer based vision models. Controlled experiments are performed using images from the Euclid Space Telescope, with three architectures being compared: a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network (CNN); a vision transformer (ViT); and a ViT fine-tuned on Euclid data. Feature embeddings are analyzed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) across multiple experiments including galaxy morphology separation, star–galaxy separation, simulated versus real observation separation, and larger randomly selected sets. The results show that transformer embeddings often produce clear separated clusters corresponding to meaningful domains. This suggests that transformer embeddings could be used as a pre- or postfiltering step in survey pipelines, reducing the volume of data that requires expensive inspection or further machine learning analysis.

blocks.html: Machine learning (ML) is widely used for analyzing astronomical survey data. Vision models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs) have been successfully applied to tasks including galaxy morphology classification [1, 2] and strong gravitational lens detection [3–5]. These methods allow large imaging datasets to be processed automatically.

Modern surveys contain extremely large numbers of images, often far exceeding what can be inspected individually. Even after ML classifications, tasks such as candidate inspection or model evaluation still require working with large subsets of the data. Methods that group visually similar objects can therefore help reduce the effective size of these datasets by allowing analysis to focus on smaller representative subsets.

Feature embeddings produced by transformer based neural networks have proven to provide a natural way to organize images, although their use for clustering and reducing large astronomical datasets remains relatively unexplored. When embedding space groups visually similar objects together, clustering can be used to identify related samples or compress large datasets into representative subsets.

In this work we analyze how embeddings from different neural network architectures cluster astronomical survey images. Using Euclid observations [6], we compare embeddings from a CNN, a general ViT, and a ViT fine-tuned on Euclid data.

In this paper, Sect. 2 describes the datasets used in the experiments. Sect. 3 outlines the model architectures and the controlled setup used to extract embeddings. Sect. 4 presents the clustering behavior observed in the different experiments. Finally, Sect. 5 discusses the application of these results for working with large astronomical datasets.

Euclid observations are obtained using two instruments: the Visible Camera (VIS) [7], providing imaging from 550–950 nm, and the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) [8], covering wavelengths from 950–2020 nm.

The experiments in this work use data from the Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) [9] together with labeled catalogs derived from the Galaxy Zoo [10–12] and Space Warps [13, 14] citizen science projects. These datasets allow clustering behavior to be evaluated across different domains, including galaxy morphologies, PSF effects, and telescope instruments.

To evaluate clustering behavior for galaxy morphology, labeled subsets of Euclid galaxies are used. The morphological labels are obtained from the Euclid Q1 visual morphology catalog [2], publicly available on the Zenodo platform<sup>1</sup>.

The catalog consists of 380 000 samples and provides morphology predictions generated using the Zoobot foundation models [15, 16]. Rather than strict labels, the catalog contains probability fractions for answers to a set of morphology questions (e.g., has-spiral-arms_yes_fraction).

In this work, classes are defined using these probability thresholds. Unless stated otherwise, a threshold of > 0.8 is used, to accommodate representative but diverse examples. Spiral galaxies are selected using spiral arm and face-on probabilities. Elliptical galaxies are selected using the smooth morphology probability, edge-on galaxies using the edge-on probability, and merging systems when the probability of a merger or disturbance > 0.7. Isolated galaxies, the counterpart for the mergers, use the probability of it being a non-merger. A star–galaxy separation filter based on the difference between peak surface brightness and total magnitude (≥−2.6) is applied in all cases.

Strong gravitational lensing is a distortion that occurs when light from a background source is deflected by a massive foreground object. These systems are a rare and powerful astrophysical class with distinctive visual structures.

To evaluate the clustering behavior for these systems, we use the Strong Lensing Discovery Engine (SLDE) catalog [17], also available on the Zenodo platform<sup>2</sup>. The catalog contains strong lens candidates identified in Euclid Q1 observations using ML models [4, 5] trained on simulated lens systems [18, 19]. After initial ranking of objects by the ML methods, highly ranked images were visually inspected by Space Warps volunteers and strong lensing experts.

Because the lens systems from the Euclid Q1 release are currently limited to 336 candidates that were successfully fit with a lens mass model, the variety of morphologies within this set is also still limited. Because this sample is too small for meaningful clustering analysis, the experiments instead compare simulated lens systems used for model training with real observational candidates. The specific simulation set [18] used for this experiment includes galaxy-galaxy lens configurations generated to match Euclid observational conditions, making them realistic and hard examples for a domain separation experiment.

Vision transformers use self-attention to learn about relationships of features in an image [20]. The experiments in this work focus on evaluating these models as a tool for clustering astronomical survey images in embedding space. To assess whether transformer representations produce meaningful structure for domain grouping, two ViT encoders are compared against a CNN.

The first transformer model is a ViT-S/16 variant. This model has 21 million trainable parameters. The second transformer model is AstroVink-Q1 [5], which uses the same ViT backbone but is fine-tuned on a set of about 130 000 galaxies captured by Euclid. AstroVink was originally developed for strong lens candidate identification, where the transformer encoder was followed by a classification head. For the experiments in this work the classification head is removed and only the encoder is used to extract embeddings. This allows comparison between representations learned by a general ViT trained on nonastronomical data and representations adapted specifically to Euclid observations.

The third model is a ResNet-50 CNN, this network contains 23 million trainable parameters and extracts image representations through convolutional layers. All three networks are pre-trained using the same DINO self-supervised strategy [21].

All experiments follow an identical pre-processing and embedding extraction procedure. Images are converted to JPEG cutouts using an arcsinh intensity stretch and resized to 256×256 pixels. Pixel values are scaled to the [0,1] range and normalized using ImageNet statistics. We only use VIS imaging, in order to maintain a consistent observational domain.

For each experiment a fixed random seed (999) is used to select a subset of images from the available dataset. Unless stated otherwise, 1 000 images are randomly sampled to construct the embedding space, with embeddings being extracted in batches of 64 images.

To obtain learned features, embeddings are extracted from the final layer of each network. For the ViT models, embeddings are taken from the class (CLS) token of the final transformer layer. The CLS token is the transformer output token used as the global image embedding. For the CNN, the global feature vector produced by the network is used as the embedding representation. The global feature vector is retrieved from the final convolutional feature maps.
To analyze the embedding space, cosine distance is used to measure similarity between embedding vectors. Cosine distance between two embeddings x and y is defined as

To visualize the structure of the embedding space, the high dimensional feature vectors are projected to two dimensions using a Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) [22]. UMAP is applied to the combined embedding sets using cosine distance, with nneighbors = 100 and mindist = 0.02.
Distances between embeddings from the two compared datasets are also computed. For each object xi, the minimum cosine distance to all samples yj in the opposite set is calculated,

where d(x, y) is the cosine distance defined above and j indexes the samples in the opposite dataset. This nearestneighbor distance measures how close each representation lies to the opposite class or domain in the embedding space.

To further analyze how reliable the clustering in an embedding space is, three metrics are used. The first is the Silhouette Coefficient [23], which measures how well two populations are separated. For each sample, the average cosine distance to samples from the same population is compared with the average cosine distance to samples from the other population. The score ranges from −1 to 1, where higher values indicate better separation and values close to or below zero indicate more overlap.

The second metric is the Neighborhood Hit (NH) [24], which measures whether similar samples belong to the same population. For each sample, NH is the fraction of its 10 most similar samples, based on cosine distance. Averaging this fraction over all samples gives an NH score from 0 to 1, where higher values suggest better grouping.

The third metric is Trustworthiness score [25], which measures how reliable the UMAP visualization is. For this, each UMAP is ran 20 times using different random seeds. Using 10 nearest neighbors, Trustworthiness checks whether samples that are close together in the UMAP are also close together in the embedding space. The score ranges from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate a more reliable projection.

Together, these three metrics describe how well the populations are separated, how dense samples from the same population are grouped together, and how reliably the UMAP projections visualizes the structure of the embedding space.

To inspect which image regions influence the representations of a transformer, attention maps are extracted from the final layer of the encoder. ViTs process an image by dividing it into small square patches, specifically 16 × 16 for the networks used in this work. In addition to these patch tokens, the CLS token is used to represent the entire image.

Rows correspond to spiral versus elliptical galaxies, merging versus isolated galaxies, edge-on versus face-on galaxies, and stars versus galaxies. Columns show embeddings from the ResNet-50 CNN, the general DINO ViT, and the Euclid fine-tuned AstroVink ViT. Points represent individual objects, while contour lines indicate the density structure of each class in the projected space. The color gradients indicate the minimum cosine distance to the nearest sample of the opposite class in the original embedding space. Darker points correspond to objects whose representations lie close to the opposite class, while brighter points indicate objects that are far from any representation of the opposite class.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The attention weights between the CLS token and all patch tokens are retrieved and averaged across attention heads. This produces an attention vector indicating which image patches contribute most strongly to the final image representation. The resulting patch attention map is reshaped to the original patch grid and resized to the full image resolution for visualization.
Figure 1 shows the UMAP projections for the morphology subsets defined in Sect. 2.2. These projections are supported numerically by the clustering verification metrics in Table 1.

blocks.caption: UMAP projections of embedding spaces for simulated lens systems and real observational candidates. Columns correspond to the ResNet-50 CNN, the general DINO ViT, and the Euclid fine-tuned AstroVink ViT encoder. Points represent individual objects, while contour lines indicate the density structure of each dataset in the projected space.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: For merging versus isolated galaxies, the CNN embeddings show strong overlap between classes, while both transformer encoders form clearer groupings. AstroVink produces the most distinct separation.

For the spiral versus elliptical galaxies, the two populations appear as separate regions in the embedding space for all three architectures. The transformer models produce more compact groupings, while the CNN representation shows broader distributions. For the edge-on versus faceon galaxies, the CNN embeddings again show limited separation between the two classes. Both transformer models form two clearly separated regions in the embedding space.

The final row shows the star–galaxy separation experiment. In this case all three architectures separate the two classes relatively well. However, the transformer embeddings again produce more clearly defined groups, while the CNN still shows overlap between clusters.

Figure 2 compares embeddings for simulated lens systems and real Euclid candidates (Sect. 2.3), supported by the clustering metrics in Table 1. The CNN embeddings show strong overlap between the two domains. The general ViT encoder shows slightly more structure but still mixes both sets. The AstroVink encoder produces a clearer shift between the simulated and observational samples, although the two domains still partially overlap.
Table 1 presents the Silhouette, NH, and Trustworthiness scores for all experiments and networks.

For the morphology experiments, NH is high for all three networks, between 0.95 and 0.99. This means that objects are usually grouped with objects from the same population. The Silhouette scores are lower, between 0.18 and 0.36, which shows that the two populations are not completely separated. This is expected because classes such as spiral, elliptical, and merging galaxies still contain substantial variation within the class itself. AstroVink-Q1 gives the highest Silhouette score in all experiments, while the NH scores are much more similar between the networks.

blocks.caption: Results on the three clustering metrics Silhouette Coefficient (SC), Neighborhood Hit (NH), and Trustworthiness Score (TC). Trustworthiness is reported as mean ± standard deviation across 20 UMAP runs.
blocks.label: Table

blocks.html: For simulated versus real lens systems, the Silhouette scores are below 0.1 and NH drops to 0.71–0.82. This weaker separation is expected because the simulated systems are drawn from real Euclid observations. The two populations therefore overlap much more strongly, although some grouping by domain is still present. This matches the overlap visible in Fig. 2.

The Trustworthiness scores range from 0.85 to 0.96, with AstroVink-Q1 giving the highest score in every experiment. The very small standard deviations, between 0.0005 and 0.0034, show that these scores remain stable across different UMAP random seeds. This supports the reliability of the UMAP visualizations.
Figure 4 shows the embedding structure for a randomly selected sample of 100 000 Euclid galaxies containing both labeled morphology classes and unlabeled objects.

The CNN embeddings form broad overlapping regions with limited structure. The general ViT encoder shows somewhat stronger grouping, while the AstroVink encoder produces the most structured organization, with spiral, elliptical, and edge-on galaxies occupying more distinct regions and stars forming a small separate cluster. Unclassified objects populate the surrounding regions of the embedding space.

To further illustrate this behavior, Fig. 3 shows eight randomly selected images sampled from the unclassified objects along a trajectory in the AstroVink embedding space between the elliptical and spiral regions defined by the labeled samples. The images show a change from smooth elliptical galaxies to objects with visible spiral structure. The corresponding attention maps indicate that the transformer focuses on prominent galaxy features such as spiral arms and central light concentrations when forming the representation.

blocks.caption: UMAP projections of embedding spaces for a randomly selected sample of 100 000 Euclid galaxies. The panels show embeddings produced by the ResNet-50 CNN encoder (left), the general DINO ViT encoder (center), and the Euclid fine-tuned AstroVink ViT encoder (right). Points correspond to individual objects with some being colored according to morphology labels.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: This work show that transformer based representations can organize astronomical imaging data into structured regions in their embedding space. While this behavior is consistent with previous work on ViTs, the results highlight a practical application for astronomical surveys.

Across multiple experiments, the ViT encoders produce dense grouping of visually similar objects. The fine-tuned AstroVink-Q1 encoder produces the most compact clusters. While this behavior is expected for a model trained on Euclid imaging data, it illustrates how domain specific finetuning can improve the structure of clusters.

Across the four morphology experiments, AstroVink-Q1 has the highest Silhouette Coefficient of the three models, and the highest NH in most cases. This indicates that fine-tuning on Euclid data improves the structure of the embedding space itself, not only the appearance of a 2D projection.

Rather than replacing existing machine learning classifiers or visual inspection campaigns, embedding-based clustering could act as a complementary step in survey pipelines. For example, embeddings could be used as a preor post-filtering stage that groups objects into visually similar subsets before further analysis. This could help reduce the number of images that require expensive processing or manual inspection by allowing classifiers or human inspection efforts to focus on representative subsets of the data.

Embedding-based organization may also be useful for structuring large catalogs by morphology. For instance, galaxy morphologies or rare object candidates could be grouped according to visual similarity, allowing related systems to be explored together rather than individually.

Future work could extend this analysis to larger datasets and additional domains. Upcoming Euclid data releases such as DR1 will contain significantly larger samples of galaxies and rare objects, allowing clustering behavior to be evaluated on more diverse astrophysical populations.
